title: Measuring How Many Turns of Crescendo Are Actually Needed

original_idea.problem: The number of Crescendo turns required for success per harm category has not been systematically characterized.
original_idea.direction: Implement Crescendo-style escalation for 5 harm categories across 3 models. Record turn-to-success. Plot distributions per category and model.
original_idea.why_it_matters: If most jailbreaks succeed within 3 turns, conversation-length limits may be insufficient. Informs tiered monitoring strategies.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain: turn count characterization -> informs conversation monitoring thresholds. The chain is reasonable but characterization alone doesn't directly fix the problem. The link to actionable defense is underspecified.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Requires implementing multi-turn Crescendo escalation, which needs careful prompt design across harm categories. Moderate complexity. Multi-turn conversation management adds overhead for beginners.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable: turn-to-success distribution per category. Clear stopping point. But implementing the escalation procedure across 5 categories requires non-trivial prompt engineering.

novelty.reasoning: The Crescendo paper (arXiv:2404.01833, USENIX Security 2025) established that Crescendo succeeds in fewer than 5 turns on average with a limit of 10 interactions, and evaluated across 4 harm categories with 12 tasks. However, the original paper used a fixed escalation strategy and did not systematically characterize per-category turn distributions across multiple models. The proposed experiment — implementing Crescendo for 5 harm categories across 3 models and plotting turn-to-success distributions — extends beyond the original paper's scope. The 'Well, that escalated quickly' single-turn Crescendo paper (arXiv:2409.03131) further explores turn efficiency. The basic characterization exists but per-category, per-model distributions are not fully mapped.
